summary: Gives system administrators guidelines for collecting and archiving evidence after a security incident, so that it can be trusted and used later. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: If something bad happens to a computer, you must save clues carefully, like a detective does. This is a how-to for gathering and keeping them safe.

questions: how to collect evidence after a security incident
what is the order of volatility
what tools do i need for incident forensics
subtitle: How a system administrator should gather and archive evidence after a security incident so that it stays trustworthy.

tldr.problem: After a security incident, the easy option is to reinstall or revert a system, which destroys evidence. Evidence that is collected badly is less useful against an attacker and may not be admissible in a prosecution.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives guiding principles, an order of volatility, a collection procedure, chain-of-custody rules for archiving, and a list of tools to prepare in advance.
tldr.outcome: Following the guidelines makes evidence much more useful for apprehending the attacker and gives it a much greater chance of being admissible.

today: RFC 3227 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 55) published in February 2002, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its tool examples reflect the practice of its time.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
A security incident, as defined in [RFC2828], is a security-relevant system event in which the system's security policy is disobeyed or otherwise breached. This RFC gives System Administrators guidelines for collecting and archiving evidence of such an incident.

The authors do not insist that guidelines be followed rigidly every time. They are guidance for administrators who elect to collect and protect information about an intrusion. Collection is a considerable effort, and faster reinstallation and reversion to a known state make the easy option more attractive, while little has been done to make archiving evidence easier.

Sites should use the guidelines as a basis for their own procedures, include them in Incident Handling documentation, and have law enforcement for their jurisdiction confirm they are adequate. The guidelines may not suit all jurisdictions.
sections.plainLanguage: Cleaning up fast is easy, but saving clues takes work. This RFC explains how to save them well if you decide to.

sections.title: Guiding Principles
sections.content:
The RFC lists principles for the whole collection effort. The main ones:

  • Follow your site's Security Policy and involve Incident Handling and Law Enforcement personnel.
  • Capture as accurate a picture of the system as possible, and minimise changes to data, including file and directory access times.
  • Keep detailed, signed and dated notes, and say whether each timestamp is UTC or local time. Note the difference between the system clock and UTC.
  • Collect first and analyse later. Proceed from the volatile to the less volatile.
  • Make a bit-level copy of the media, and do any forensics on a copy of that copy, since analysis will almost certainly alter access times.
  • Test procedures so they are implementable in a crisis, and automate them if possible. Work step by step on one system, but spread several devices across the team.

Administrators should be prepared to testify, perhaps years later, about every action and when it happened.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down everything you do and when, change as little as you can, and save the clues before you study them. Work on a copy of the copy.

sections.title: Order of Volatility and Things to Avoid
sections.content:
The order of volatility says what to collect first. The RFC's example order for a typical system runs: registers and cache; routing table, arp cache, process table, kernel statistics and memory; temporary file systems; disk; remote logging and monitoring data; physical configuration and network topology; and archival media.

It is easy to destroy evidence inadvertently. The RFC warns against these:

  • Shutting down before collection is complete, since evidence may be lost and the attacker may have altered startup and shutdown scripts.
  • Trusting the programs on the system. Run collection tools from appropriately protected media.
  • Running programs such as tar or xcopy that modify the access time of all files.
  • Simply disconnecting or filtering the system from the network, which may trigger "deadman switches" that wipe evidence.
sections.plainLanguage: Ice cream melts faster than a rock, so grab the ice cream first. And do not switch off the lights or trust the burglar's tools.

sections.title: Privacy and Legal Considerations
sections.content:
Collectors must respect the privacy rules of their company and legal jurisdiction. Nothing collected alongside the evidence, such as log files that may reveal user behaviour or personal data files, should be available to anyone who would not normally have access. Administrators should not intrude without strong justification, should not collect from areas such as personal file stores unless there is sufficient indication of a real incident, and should have the backing of established company procedures.

For legal purposes computer evidence needs to be admissible, authentic, complete, reliable and believable. In short, it must meet court rules, be tied to the incident, tell the whole story, be free of doubt about how it was handled, and be understandable to a court.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not snoop through people's private things unless there is a real reason, and make sure the clues you keep are the kind a judge would trust.

sections.title: The Collection Procedure
sections.content:
Collection procedures should be as detailed and unambiguous as possible, minimising the decision-making needed in the moment. The methods should be transparent and reproducible, and testable by independent experts.

The listed steps: identify which systems hold evidence; decide what is likely to be relevant and admissible, erring on the side of collecting too much; get the order of volatility for each system; remove external avenues for change; collect in that order with the prepared tools; record the extent of the system's clock drift; question what else may be evidence; document each step; and note the people involved and what they observed.

Where feasible, generate checksums and cryptographically sign the collected evidence to help preserve a strong chain of evidence, without altering the evidence.
sections.plainLanguage: Make a clear checklist ahead of time, follow it step by step, write down who was there, and stamp each clue so you can show it was not changed.

sections.title: Archiving and Chain of Custody
sections.content:
Evidence must be strictly secured, and the chain of custody must be clearly documented. It should be possible to describe how the evidence was found, how it was handled and everything that happened to it.

Document where, when and by whom evidence was discovered and collected; where, when and by whom it was handled or examined; who had custody and for what period, and how it was stored; and, whenever custody changed, when and how the transfer happened, including shipping numbers.

For storage, use commonly used media rather than obscure media if possible. Access should be extremely restricted and clearly documented, and unauthorised access should be detectable.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a logbook of who held each clue and when, lock the clues up, and make sure you would notice if someone sneaked a look.

sections.title: Tools You Need
sections.content:
Prepare the programs for evidence collection and forensics on read-only media such as a CD, for each Operating System you manage, before you need them. The set should include a program for examining processes (for example ps), programs for system state (for example ifconfig, netstat, arp), a bit-to-bit copy program (for example dd), programs for checksums and signatures (for example sha1sum, pgp), programs for core images (for example gcore, gdb), and scripts to automate collection such as The Coroner's Toolkit.

The tools should be statically linked and need no libraries other than those on the read-only media. Even so, since modern rootkits may be installed through loadable kernel modules, the tools might not give a full picture of the system. Administrators should be ready to testify to the authenticity and reliability of the tools they use.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a toolbox on a disc that cannot be changed, so a burglar cannot tamper with your tools. Even then, remember a clever burglar might hide things from them.
